meta_home_title: EpiDetective — Open tools for reading health evidence
meta_home_desc: A personal project by Wenxin Wan, a cancer epidemiologist: free tools to look up what published research says causes cancer and other chronic diseases, and how sure the evidence is. Cancer data: IARC Monographs.
meta_explorer_desc: See which exposures have been linked to which cancers, and how strong the evidence is for each link. Data: IARC Monographs, Classifications by cancer site (Vols 1–141). A personal project by Wenxin Wan.
home_h1: What causes cancer and other chronic diseases, and how sure the evidence is
home_personal: A personal project by Wenxin Wan, a cancer epidemiologist. Free tools built from the IARC Monographs and from published reviews. They describe whole populations; they cannot tell you what caused any one person’s illness.
home_audience: For the curious public, clinicians, students and journalists.

qa_label: Four questions, answered from the tools
qa_a1: In June 2023 IARC classified aspartame as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B), a rating of hazard. WHO says a 70-kilogram adult would need more than 9 to 14 cans of diet drink a day to pass [the acceptable daily intake].
qa_q2: Is processed meat as bad as smoking?
qa_a2: Each 50 grams eaten every day raises the risk of bowel cancer by 18%. In European data, about 10 to 12 in 100 smokers get lung cancer by age 75, compared with 4 to 5 in 1,000 lifelong non-smokers.
qa_q3: Does my job raise my cancer risk?
qa_k3: 68 workplace agents and jobs are on the cancer map, from asbestos and silica dust to night-shift work and firefighting.
qa_a3: Painters with over 10 years in the trade had about 1.8 times the bladder-cancer risk of non-painters. Lung-cancer risk rises with the total silica breathed over the years.
qa_go3: Work and cancer, sector by sector →
qa_k4: Twelve risk factors are graded for ischaemic stroke, from blood pressure, smoking and diabetes (Strong) to depression (Suggestive).
qa_a4: Blood pressure is the single largest modifiable contributor to stroke worldwide.

inst_t1_desc: See which exposures have been linked to which cancers, and how strong the evidence is behind each link. Its data come from the IARC Monographs, in which independent Working Groups convened by IARC evaluate what can cause cancer. Start from a cancer, start from an exposure, or open the whole map. Counted here: every agent for which IARC’s cancer-site table lists at least limited evidence in people for a named cancer (Volumes 1 to 141), adapted as the tool describes.
inst_t2_desc: Which risk factors have been linked to heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, dementia and other major chronic conditions, and how strong the evidence is behind each link, including where studies disagree. Cancer has its own explorer. Open the network to see how the risk factors group together.
about_h2: Built by a cancer epidemiologist who uses this evidence in his research.
about_p1: I am Wenxin Wan, a postdoctoral scientist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the World Health Organization’s cancer agency, based in Lyon, France.
about_p2: I obtained my MSc in Epidemiology from the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom and my PhD from Utrecht University in the Netherlands, where I studied how exposures at work and in the environment shape cancer risk at the population level. My research on occupational benzene exposure and lung cancer has been published in leading journals, including Environmental Health Perspectives and the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine (2024), with findings also cited in The New York Times.
about_p3: My daily work at IARC revolves around large international cohorts: millions of people followed over many years so that the risk factors causally linked to disease can be identified. I lead the analysis and coordinate the project for OPICO, the international opioid cohort consortium, which brings ten cohorts from three continents together to ask what cancer risk long-term opioid use may carry; and I serve as scientific advisor to the Lung Cancer Cohort Consortium (LC3), helping carry the evidence built up by occupational-exposure research into lung cancer screening for populations worldwide.
about_p4: I’ve spent years contributing to scientific research, yet much of the evidence we produce never reaches the people who could benefit from it. I created EpiDetective to help bridge that gap, making scientific evidence more accessible, understandable, and relevant to everyday life.

exp_h1: Some exposures are known to cause cancer. Others are only suspected. This map shows which is which.
exp_lede: The dots and lines behind this heading are the dataset itself: 185 exposures, 68 types of cancer and the 469 links between them, taken from the IARC Monographs table “Classifications by cancer site”. Counted here: every agent for which that table lists at least limited evidence in people for a named cancer (Volumes 1 to 141), adapted as the tool describes.
exp_whatsin_h2: The exposures IARC has linked to a cancer, graded by how certain the evidence is.
exp_bar1_note: Studies in people show a link, and chance, bias and confounding have been ruled out with reasonable confidence. This is the strongest conclusion IARC draws from studies in people.
exp_bar2_note: A causal link is credible, but chance, bias or confounding could not be ruled out with reasonable confidence. More research may settle it either way.
exp_reads_h2: Three things to know before you read the map.
exp_read1_h3: Something that can cause cancer may still have had nothing to do with yours.
exp_read1_p: A Group 1 classification means an exposure can cause cancer under some conditions. How much, for how long, at what age, and which genes you carry all stand between that finding and any one person.
exp_read2_h3: A missing link may only mean nobody has looked hard enough yet.
exp_read2_p: The map records what has been studied and reviewed. Many gaps come from limited research funding or short follow-up time, so an empty space here is weak evidence of safety.
exp_read3_h3: This map describes populations, and cannot judge any single case.
exp_read3_p: If you are living with a cancer diagnosis, the people treating you know things about your case that no population map contains. Bring your questions to them.
exp_cta_h2: Start from a cancer or an exposure, or open the whole map.
exp_cta_lede: Free, in ten languages. Drag, zoom, and focus on any part of the network.
exp_cta_source: Source: IARC Monographs, “Classifications by cancer site”, Volumes 1–141 (last update 18 May 2026), adapted from Schubauer-Berigan et al., JNCI Monographs 2026, and augmented for later evaluations and for the single HPV types named in Volume 100B. This tool identifies hazards across whole populations. For anything concerning your own health, speak to a doctor.

meta_games_title: Cancer awareness games — skin, lung and breast — EpiDetective
meta_games_desc: Three free browser games about cancer prevention: sun safety for ages 6 to 12, what causes lung cancer for ages 10 to 16, and breast cancer for 14 and up.
games_sub: A side-scrolling adventure that teaches children how to enjoy the sun without harming their skin.
games_p1: Most skin cancers are caused by ultraviolet radiation, and the habits that prevent them are learned young. In this game Sol runs, jumps and collects sun stars across five regions, from a grassy meadow to a snowy mountain. Along the way Sol picks up a broad-brimmed hat and SPF 30+ sunscreen, loses the sunscreen after a swim, and reaches checkpoints where a quiz question must be answered before the path opens again.
games_p2: The questions cover what the UV Index means, when protection matters (UV 3 and above), why shade, clothing and sunscreen work best together, how sand, water and snow reflect UV, and why tanning beds should be avoided. Wrong answers are never punished: Sol is nudged back with a hint and a laugh. The game runs in your browser, works on a phone, and collects no data. It is in English.
games_fact_questions: questions in the bank, 5 per run
games_step1: Press Play. On a keyboard, move with A D or ← → and jump with Space. On a phone, use the on-screen buttons. A game controller works too.
games_step2: Collect sun coins and the nine hidden sun stars. Some platforms move and some fall, springs send Sol high, and the small animals on the path can be hopped over or bounced on.
games_step3: Watch the UV Index and the sun meter in the top bar. The UV Index changes from region to region and drops when Sol stands in shade. The sun meter fills in strong sun and empties in shade; a hat and sunscreen slow it down, and sunscreen wears off, so look for a bottle to reapply it.
games_step4: At each checkpoint, read the question and jump up beneath one of the three answer blocks. The right answer opens the gate; a wrong one gives a hint and another try.
games_step5: Press <kbd>R</kbd> to restart. The cog opens the settings: voice narration, high contrast, a dyslexia-friendly font, larger text, game speed and touch-control size.
games_regions_h: The five regions and their UV Index
games_fine: The game uses an original character and artwork. Its source is open at github.com/Wenxin-Wan/sun-safety-adventure. The sun-safety advice follows the European Code Against Cancer and WHO guidance on UV protection.
games_cap: Screenshot of the game as it runs
games_shot_alt: The game as it runs: Sol on a grassy platform, the UV Index in the top bar, coins and sun stars ahead.
games_shelf_h2: Three are open now: one each for skin, lung and breast.
games_g1_desc: A platform adventure about sun safety for children aged 6 to 12. Five regions, a quiz at each checkpoint, and a shield kit of hat, cover-up, shade and sunscreen to assemble along the way.
games_over_lede: Each game teaches one part of cancer prevention through play. They run in the browser, collect no data, and show the source behind everything they say. Choose one to see how it is played and what it teaches.
games_g2_sub: An investigation across a flat, a street and a building yard, in which every clue is filed in one of IARC’s groups.
games_g2_p1: Smoking causes most lung cancers, and stopping helps at whatever age it happens. That is the first finding in the case file, and the rest of the investigation builds on it. The player searches three scenes, a flat, a street and a building yard, and turns up twelve clues. Each has to be filed in the group IARC gives it: a known cause of lung cancer (Group 1), a probable cause (Group 2A), a possible cause (Group 2B), or not classifiable, which means the evidence is too limited to say (Group 3). The real hazards can then be fixed, and a clean-air score rises with each one.
games_g2_p2: The clues cover second-hand smoke; radon in the home, with a small detector game built around the WHO reference level of 100 Bq/m³; outdoor air pollution and diesel exhaust; wood smoke and high-temperature frying; and the silica dust, asbestos and welding fumes of a building site. Bitumen roofing lands in the probable group, and hot mastic asphalt laid on a pavement in the possible group. Coffee is not classifiable, because the evidence is too limited to say. A poster claiming that stress causes cancer is a myth to check: IARC has never evaluated stress, and a large study of workers found no clear link with lung cancer. Three conversations carry the argument: a flatmate who smokes only a few a day, a vape-shop owner who calls vaping harmless, and a foreman who thinks quitting after twenty years is pointless. Every clue shows its source and the official wording of the European Code Against Cancer. The game runs in your browser, works on a phone, and collects no data. It is in English.
games_g2_step1: Press Play, then search each scene for its four clues. A ring appears when the pointer passes over one. On a phone, tap whatever looks suspicious: a miss tells you whether you are warm or cold. Tab and Enter work too, and a hint button shows one clue.
games_g2_step2: File each clue in one of four drawers, by IARC’s groups: known cause (Group 1), probable cause (Group 2A), possible cause (Group 2B) or not classifiable (Group 3). A wrong drawer is greyed out and you try again; the right one opens the source and the wording of the European Code Against Cancer. The street also holds a myth to check. It has no drawer: you read it and press Noted.
games_g2_step3: Fix the hazards that can be fixed. Each one raises the clean-air score. In the flat, the radon detector is a small game of its own: the WHO reference level is 100 Bq/m³, and WHO says national reference levels should not exceed 300.
games_g2_step4: Talk to the three people you meet: the flatmate, the vape-shop owner and the foreman. Each has a reason to doubt, and you answer with the evidence.
games_g2_step5: After the third case comes the line-up: six clues to file again from memory. The report then gives your detective rank and the clean-air score. The cog opens the settings: high contrast, larger text, wider and easier-to-read letters, reduced motion, sound, and an option to show where the clues are.
games_g2_fine: Every clue in the game cites its source. The classifications follow the IARC Monographs, the prevention wording is that of the European Code Against Cancer, and the radon reference level is the WHO’s (100 Bq/m³). The finding that stopping smoking helps at any age comes from Peto and colleagues (BMJ, 2000).
games_g2_desc: An investigation game about what causes lung cancer, for ages 10 to 16. Three scenes, twelve clues to file as known cause, probable cause, possible cause or not classifiable, a radon detector to read, and three people to talk round.
games_g2_cap: Screenshot of The Lung Detective as it runs
games_g2_shot_alt: The Lung Detective as it runs: one of the three scenes, with rings on the clues found so far and the detective’s notebook below.
games_g3_sub: A choices game in which a town council follows 1,000 women from their twenties to their sixties and sees, dot by dot, what prevention changes.
games_g3_p1: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, and much of what is said about preventing it rests on very little. In this game the player is the council of a town whose 1,000 women are followed from their twenties to their sixties. Each of five chapters brings two decision cards and a small effort budget to spend on them: alcohol, physical activity, weight after the menopause, breastfeeding, menopausal hormone therapy, screening. The outcome appears on an array of 1,000 dots as the number of women diagnosed with breast cancer by age 75, about 94 of 1,000 in Western Europe (GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates), and the number who die of it, about 15.
games_g3_p2: The effect sizes are modest, taken from pooled studies, so a good decade of choices moves a handful of dots. Myth cards are there to be spotted: antiperspirants and underwired bras cost effort and change nothing, and a smoke-free card explains that for breast cancer the evidence on smoking is limited, whatever smoking does elsewhere in the body. The game ends with a panel headed “What this game can and cannot say”: these are population averages, and they predict nothing about any one woman. It runs in your browser, works on a phone, and collects no data. It is in English.
games_g3_step1: Press Play. You sit as the council of a town whose 1,000 women you will follow across five decades, one chapter for each decade of their lives.
games_g3_step2: Each chapter deals two decision cards and gives you a small effort budget. Read both cards, then spend the budget where you think it will count.
games_g3_step3: Before each count, forecast how far the decade’s choices will move the number diagnosed. Then watch the 1,000 dots: each choice moves the number of women diagnosed by age 75, and the number who die of it, by the amount the pooled studies support. Small movements are what the evidence supports.
games_g3_step4: Some cards are myths. Antiperspirants and underwired bras cost effort and move nothing; the smoke-free card explains why the breast-cancer evidence for smoking is only limited.
games_g3_step5: At the end, compare your town with a council that did nothing and with the most any council could do, then read the panel “What this game can and cannot say”. The numbers are averages for a population like Western Europe’s, and no dot stands for any one woman.
games_g3_fine: Baseline figures are for Western Europe (GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates). Effect sizes come from pooled studies of alcohol, physical activity, weight after the menopause, breastfeeding, menopausal hormone therapy and screening participation. The prevention advice follows the European Code Against Cancer.
games_g3_desc: A choices game about breast cancer prevention, for ages 14 and up. Five chapters, ten decision cards, a small effort budget, and 1,000 dots that show how many women a town’s choices spare.
games_g3_cap: Screenshot of A Town of 1,000 as it runs
games_g3_shot_alt: A Town of 1,000 as it runs: the 1,000-dot array with the affected women marked, and the chapter’s two decision cards.

meta_reading_title: How to read health evidence — EpiDetective
meta_reading_desc: Seven ideas that make a health headline easier to weigh: hazard and risk, relative and absolute risk, association and cause, chance and bias, the range around an estimate, what “no evidence” means, and populations and people. With a worked example and the labels of both tools side by side.
read_h1: Seven ideas that make health evidence readable.
read_lede: Every number in the tools on this site rests on a few ideas from epidemiology. None of them needs mathematics. Read them once and a health headline becomes much easier to weigh.
read_1_h3: A hazard is something that can cause harm. Risk is how likely the harm is.
read_1_p: Sunlight, alcohol and asbestos are all hazards: each can cause cancer. How likely that is for any one person depends on how much, for how long and at what age. The IARC Monographs identify hazards and leave the size of the risk to other studies.
read_2_h3: “Twice the risk” means little until you know twice what.
read_2_p: A relative risk compares two groups. An absolute risk says how many people are affected. Doubling a risk of 1 in 10,000 adds one case among 10,000 people; a 10% rise in a risk of 1 in 10 adds a hundred among the same 10,000. Ask for both numbers.
read_3_h3: Two things can rise together without one causing the other.
read_3_p: People who carry a lighter develop more lung cancer, and the lighter is innocent: smoking explains both. Epidemiologists call this confounding. Before they call a link causal, they look for the same result across many studies, for more disease where there is more exposure, and for the exposure coming first.
read_4_h3: Every estimate comes with a range, and the range is part of the result.
read_4_p: A study might report a relative risk of 1.2 with a 95% confidence interval from 0.9 to 1.6. The data fit a small increase, and they fit no effect at all just as well, because the interval includes 1. A narrow interval from a large study deserves more weight than a wide one from a small study.
read_5_tag: No evidence, and evidence of no effect
read_5_h3: “We could not tell” and “it is safe” are two different findings.
read_5_p: When IARC places an agent in Group 3, “not classifiable”, the studies were usually too few or too weak to decide either way. That describes the state of the evidence. Group 3 is also used when strong evidence shows that the way an agent causes cancer in animals does not operate in people, and nothing else supports a higher group. Since the 2019 Preamble, IARC no longer has a Group 4 (“probably not carcinogenic”), and agents that would once have gone there now go in Group 3. Showing that something is safe takes large, careful studies that looked for harm and found none.
read_6_h3: These numbers describe groups. They cannot explain one person’s illness.
read_6_p: A risk factor shifts the odds across thousands of people. Most people with a given exposure never develop the disease, and some people without it do. For anything about your own health, ask the people treating you.
read_cta_h2: Open a tool and read the evidence for yourself.
read_home_h2: Seven ideas that make a health headline easier to weigh.
read_home_lede: Hazard and risk, relative and absolute risk, association and cause, and four more. A five-minute read, with no mathematics.

meta_hwc_desc: Where the data in EpiDetective’s two tools come from, how they were checked, which version is online, and how to report an error. A personal project by Wenxin Wan.
hwc_h1: Where the data come from, how they were checked, and how to report an error.
hwc_lede: EpiDetective is a personal project by Wenxin Wan. This page lists the sources behind the two tools, the checks they went through and the versions now online. If you find a mistake, the last section says how to report it.
hwc_src_c1: IARC Monographs, table “Classifications by cancer site”, Volumes 1–141 (last update 18 May 2026): the 185 agents with at least limited evidence in people for a named cancer, and their 469 links to 68 types of cancer. Adapted from Schubauer-Berigan et al., JNCI Monographs 2026, and augmented for later evaluations and for the single HPV types named in Volume 100B.
hwc_src_c2: IARC Monographs, List of Classifications, Volumes 1–142 (last updated 23 July 2026): the group of each agent, and the 874 agents IARC evaluated without naming a cancer site.
hwc_src_c3: The evaluation in each agent’s Monograph volume: what IARC found in studies of people, in studies of experimental animals and on how the agent acts in the body.
hwc_src_k1: Systematic reviews with meta-analysis, pooled cohort consortia and expert syntheses, such as the GBD Burden of Proof analyses and the Lancet Commissions. A single study is used only as randomised or genetic evidence that supports or contradicts a finding from observational studies.
hwc_src_k2: The reference index lists the 641 published sources behind the links, each with a link to the paper.
hwc_chk_c1: Every link was compared with IARC’s cancer-site table. Where the table lists a cancer that the evaluation text of the volume does not name, the entry says so.
hwc_chk_c2: The volume and year behind each classification were checked against IARC’s List of Classifications and the Monograph volumes, in two independent passes (October 2026). The evidence in people, in animals and on how each agent acts was taken from IARC’s own evaluations, checked in a second pass, and every quote compared with its source.
hwc_chk_c3: IARC’s List of Classifications was last compared with the tool on 28 October 2026. It had not changed since IARC’s update of 23 July 2026.
hwc_chk_k1: Every effect estimate was compared with the paper it cites, for the exact comparison stated (August 2026). In September 2026 a second pass checked 100 flagged links against their papers again. Each grade follows the written decision table of the framework.
hwc_chk_k2: The change log records every change to every link since the first published version (24 August 2026). In it, 343 of the 431 links now in the tool have at least one dated check or correction from September or October 2026. The log lists changes only, so a link that was checked and found correct leaves no row: more links were checked than this count shows.
hwc_link_framework: Framework: what has been checked and what has not
hwc_chk_ai: The author ran the checks with AI-assisted verification: AI models compared each value with its source, and the author reviewed the results and made the corrections. No outside expert has reviewed the Chronic Disease Evidence Explorer’s estimates or grades.
hwc_ver_c_data: Data: IARC’s cancer-site table, last update 18 May 2026, and IARC’s List of Classifications, last updated 23 July 2026.
hwc_ver_k_data: 356 graded links and 75 related-outcome links. Version 2.0 renamed the grades and sets each one by a written decision table.
hwc_not_p: It is a personal project. It is no IARC or WHO product, no risk assessment, and no medical advice.
hwc_not_p2: The tools show what published research says about large groups of people. They cannot tell you what caused any one person’s illness. For your own health, talk to a doctor.
hwc_rep_p: Write to epidetective@gmail.com. The button below opens an email with four lines to fill in:
hwc_rep_reply: You will get an answer, usually within two weeks.
meta_work_desc: 68 workplace agents and jobs that IARC has linked to a cancer, grouped by sector, with IARC’s label, the cancers concerned and a link to each entry. A personal project by Wenxin Wan.
work_h1: Work and cancer: what IARC has found, sector by sector.
work_lede: 68 workplace agents and jobs that IARC has linked to a cancer, grouped by sector. Each row shows IARC’s label, the number of cancer links and a link to the full entry. The sector grouping is EpiDetective’s; IARC lists agents alphabetically.
work_note: A label says how sure IARC is that something can cause cancer. Your own risk depends on the dose, the years of exposure and the protection at work.
work_find: Not on this page? The cancer tool’s search covers all 185 agents on the map, and the 874 others IARC evaluated without naming a cancer site.
work_ecac_official: The official text, quoted as published.
work_ecac_rendering: The Code has no official edition in this language. Below is EpiDetective’s rendering of the official text.
work_beyond_h2: Eight workplace risks for other chronic diseases.
work_beyond_p: Work is also linked to heart, lung, kidney and joint disease. The Chronic Disease Evidence Explorer grades how sure the evidence is that each risk factor causes a disease, and eight of its risk factors come from work. Its grades are its own and differ from IARC’s labels.
lbl_h2: The labels in both tools, side by side.
lbl_lede: The two tools answer “how sure is the evidence?” with three sets of labels. For each label, the table says what it claims, what it leaves open and the official term behind it.
lbl_cap_cause: How sure IARC is that an agent can cause cancer
lbl_cap_link: What studies in people show for one cancer
lbl_cap_chronic: How sure the evidence is that a risk factor causes a disease
lbl_g1_says: The agent can cause cancer in people. This is the group in which IARC is most certain.
lbl_g1_not: How large the risk is, or at what dose. Processed meat and tobacco smoking are both in Group 1, with very different risks.
lbl_g2a_says: The agent probably causes cancer in people. The evidence falls short of Group 1, most often because the studies in people are limited.
lbl_g2a_not: That it causes cancer at the levels people usually meet, or how large any risk is.
lbl_g2b_says: The agent may cause cancer in people. One kind of evidence points that way, such as limited evidence in people or sufficient evidence in animals.
lbl_g2b_not: That it probably causes cancer, or that people exposed to it are at risk.
lbl_g3_says: The evidence does not meet the rules for any other group, usually because there is too little of it.
lbl_g3_not: That it is safe. Group 3 describes the state of the evidence.
lbl_g3_term: Not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans (Group 3)
lbl_est_says: Studies in people show that it causes this cancer. Chance, bias and confounding were ruled out with reasonable confidence.
lbl_est_not: How large the risk is, or whether it caused a particular person’s cancer.
lbl_est_term: Sufficient evidence of carcinogenicity in humans
lbl_sus_says: Studies in people show a link with this cancer, and a causal link is credible. Chance, bias or confounding could not be ruled out.
lbl_sus_not: That it causes this cancer. More research may confirm the link or rule it out.
lbl_sus_term: Limited evidence of carcinogenicity in humans
lbl_strong_says: Different kinds of evidence agree that this is a cause, and a reversal is unlikely.
lbl_strong_not: How large the effect is. A Strong link can carry a small effect; the estimate in the panel gives the size.
lbl_moderate_says: Probably a cause: studies agree and show a gradient or a known mechanism, but one strand of proof is still missing.
lbl_moderate_not: That the question is settled. The missing strand of proof could confirm the link or overturn it.
lbl_suggestive_says: A consistent association, but confounding or reverse causation has not been ruled out.
lbl_suggestive_not: That the factor causes the disease. Another factor, or an early stage of the disease itself, may explain the link.
lbl_weak_says: A signal from few, inconsistent or bias-prone studies. It may not hold up.
lbl_weak_not: That the factor has no effect. The studies are too few, too inconsistent or too prone to bias to say much either way.
lbl_conflicting_says: Good evidence points in opposite directions, often observational studies against trials or genetic studies.
lbl_conflicting_not: Which side is right. The panel shows which kinds of study point which way.
lbl_chronic_term: No official term. These five grades belong to the Chronic Disease Evidence Explorer, which defines them in its framework. None of them is an IARC category.
lbl_old_says: Convincing → Strong · Probable → Moderate · Limited → Weak · Contested → Conflicting. Suggestive kept its name.
lbl_old_not: That a link kept its grade. Version 2.0 also re-graded some links, and the change log lists each one.
lbl_old_term: Names used until version 2.0, published on 23 October 2026
lbl_hazard_note: A hazard says whether something can cause harm. A hazard ratio is a study’s number comparing how fast harm happens in two groups. The words look alike and mean different things.
read_7_h3: A result can come from luck, or lean one way because of how the study was run.
read_7_p1: Chance. Every study looks at a sample of people, and a small sample can show a link, or hide one, by luck alone. Toss a fair coin ten times and you get seven heads or more about one time in six; toss it a thousand times and the share of heads stays close to half. That is why one small study rarely settles a question.
read_7_p2: Bias. A study can lean one way because of how it was run. The Interphone study asked people to recall their past mobile phone use, and heavy users tended to overestimate theirs. IARC said chance or bias may explain the higher risk of glioma, a brain tumour, seen in the heaviest users.
read_see_how: Two numbers, and what each one means
read_see_redmeat: Unprocessed red meat and coronary heart disease
read_ex_h2: One headline, read with the seven ideas.
read_ex_lede: Headlines like this one followed IARC’s evaluation of red and processed meat in October 2015. Here is the same news, read with each idea in turn.
read_ex_1: IARC placed processed meat in Group 1, its most certain group, because the evidence in people is sufficient for bowel cancer. That answers whether it can cause cancer. How much it raises the risk is a separate question.
read_ex_2: The tool’s entry says: “Each 50 grams eaten every day raises the risk of bowel cancer by 18%.” That is a relative risk. Tobacco smoking is in Group 1 too, and its entry gives absolute numbers: “In European data, about 10 to 12 in 100 smokers get lung cancer by age 75, compared with 4 to 5 in 1,000 lifelong non-smokers.” Same certainty, very different size.
read_ex_3: People who eat a lot of processed meat may also differ in other ways, for example in how much they smoke or exercise. A verdict of sufficient evidence means IARC’s Working Group judged, with reasonable confidence, that such differences do not explain the link.
read_ex_7: The same verdict means chance and bias were ruled out with reasonable confidence too. That judgement weighs the whole body of studies. A single small study could not carry it.
read_ex_4: The 18% is a central estimate from pooled studies, and like every estimate it comes with a range. Ask for the range before you weigh the number: if it includes no effect, the data also fit no rise at all.
read_ex_5: IARC’s verdict covers processed meat and, in Group 2A, red meat. Other foods were outside this evaluation, so the headline says nothing about whether they are safe.
read_ex_6: These figures describe large groups. They cannot tell anyone whether a particular bowel cancer came from eating ham. Most people who eat processed meat never get bowel cancer, and some who never eat it do.
read_more_1: The IARC Monographs Preamble (amended January 2019): the rules IARC follows to weigh the evidence and assign its groups.
read_more_2: Causal Inference: What If, by Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins (2020): a free textbook on telling cause from association.
read_quiz_hint: Think of an answer first, then open the question to compare.
read_q1: Sunlight and processed meat are both in IARC’s Group 1. Are they equally dangerous?
read_a1: No. Group 1 says the evidence that each can cause cancer is equally sure. How much each one raises the risk is a separate question, and the answers differ widely.
read_q2: A headline says a food “doubles the risk” of a rare cancer. What do you need to know before you worry?
read_a2: How common the cancer is to begin with. Doubling a risk of 1 in 10,000 adds one case among 10,000 people.
read_q3: Towns that sell more ice cream have more drownings. Does ice cream cause drowning?
read_a3: No. Hot weather brings both: people eat more ice cream and swim more. A third factor that drives two things at once is called a confounder.
read_q4: A study reports a relative risk of 1.3, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.8 to 2.1. Has it shown that the risk goes up?
read_a4: No. The interval includes 1, so the data also fit no change in risk. A larger study would narrow the range.
read_q5: IARC places an agent in Group 3, “not classifiable”. Can you say it is safe?
read_a5: No. Group 3 means the evidence was too limited to decide. Showing that something is safe takes large studies that looked for harm and found none.
exp_eval_p: Search also finds the 874 other agents IARC has evaluated without naming a cancer site, such as coffee (Group 3). Each one shows its group, the volume and year of the evaluation, and a link to IARC’s list.
exp_streams_p: Each of the 185 entries also sets out the three kinds of evidence IARC weighs: studies in people, studies in experimental animals, and evidence on how the agent acts in the body.
exp_lbl_h2: Every entry carries one of IARC’s four groups.
exp_lbl_p: The group says how sure IARC is that an agent can cause cancer in people. It says nothing about how large the risk is, which depends on the dose and the circumstances.
exp_lbl_totals: IARC’s own totals for every agent it has classified, from its List of Classifications (Volumes 1–142, last updated 23 July 2026). The map holds agents from Groups 1, 2A and 2B; Group 3 agents are found by search.
